description:
ASTRAtegy – Where creativity meets engineering.

We are a two-person team combining a passion for creativity, technology, and exploration. One of us comes from a Computer Science background, bringing technical thinking and programming skills, while the other brings a creative perspective, with an interest in design, storytelling, and turning complex ideas into engaging experiences.
summary: Space Mission Simulator is a 3D browser game in which players design and fly a real space mission, alone or as a crew of up to four. Players pick one of five missions inspired by the challenge resources (PUNCH, PILOT, a lunar ice CubeSat, Dawn and a Mars-moon sample return), then build the spacecraft step by step: size, instruments, power, engine, orbit, launch vehicle and antenna. Every choice changes six live resources (budget, mass, power, data, communications and time), and a Go/No-Go poll blocks the launch until the design is feasible. In flight, players face real-world problems with a 30-second clock, and their design decides which choices are safe. After every decision, the mascot Commander Catstronaut explains the real science and the real mission behind it, and a final report shows why the mission succeeded or failed. This addresses the challenge because it lets anyone experience a complete mission, from objective to operations, and understand the trade-offs that connect its parts, rather than studying orbits, rockets or budgets in isolation.
details:
What does it do?

The game guides players through a complete mission life cycle in three phases:

  • Phase 1: Spacecraft Design. Players select a mission objective, review its requirements (such as carrying an ice detector, reaching a target velocity change, staying within budget, and returning at least 70% of the data), and make one key decision across eight steps. As components are added, a 3D model of the spacecraft builds in real time while six resource bars track the trade-offs of every choice.
  • Phase 2: Pre-Launch Check. Four specialized roles—Scientist, Engineer, Launch Lead, and Ground Lead—each monitor a console that reports GO or NO-GO based on their own metrics. The mission can only launch once all four consoles report GO, triggering an animated 3D launch with the selected rocket.
  • Phase 3: Flight and Debrief. Across seven flight milestones (launch, journey, arrival, three science phases, and data downlink), players face random real-world anomalies drawn from a pool of 28 events, alongside timed crises where every role must respond simultaneously. Outcomes depend on both player knowledge and spacecraft design (spare power, budget reserve, engine type, lifetime, and link margin). Wrong calls damage the spacecraft, and if health drops below 40%, the mission fails. After each decision, Commander Catstronaut explains the science using historical spaceflight examples (such as Apollo 12's lightning strike, Kepler's reaction wheels, Dawn's bright spots on Ceres, and Philae's bounce on Comet 67P). Optional hints are available at the cost of points. A final debrief report breaks down the score (science, objectives, budget saved, crew goals, bonuses, and difficulty multiplier), compares the player's build against the real mission, and logs results on a local leaderboard so players can redesign and fly again.

How does it work?

A lightweight mission engine calculates cost, mass, power, data volume, link capacity, lifetime, and launch feasibility (applying the rocket equation with a fuel margin and verifying launch mass against rocket capacity for the target orbit). This unified engine drives all GO/NO-GO checks, flight event outcomes, and final scoring. The entire application runs client-side in a single HTML file—requiring no installation, backend server, or user account.

What benefits does it have?

  • Tangible Systems Thinking: Turns abstract aerospace trade-offs into immediate, visible consequences and teaches players why an engineering decision works rather than simply marking it right or wrong.
  • Dual-Level Accessibility: Welcomes beginners with step-by-step mascot guidance, optional hints, and approachable numbers, while still offering deep strategic trade-offs for advanced players.
  • Solo and Collaborative Modes: Supports both single-player and same-screen team play, using competing role objectives and timed crises to encourage active communication and crew coordination.

What do you hope to achieve? Our primary goal is that anyone who plays for ten minutes can clearly explain why their mission succeeded or failed. Planned next steps include adding selectable difficulty levels, an open sandbox mode, save-and-compare functionality for spacecraft designs, and multi-device support where each crew member uses their own phone as a live mission control console.

Tools, languages, and software

  • Frontend and 3D Engine: HTML5, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js (r128) for real-time 3D graphics (procedural spacecraft and rocket models, shader-based atmospheres and skyboxes, and particle effects).
  • Audio and Storage: Web Audio API for cockpit alerts and alarms; browser localStorage for saving settings and high scores.
  • Asset Pipeline and Testing: Python (Pillow, NumPy) for converting and compressing NASA 3D models and textures; Python and Playwright with headless Chrome for automated playthrough testing.
  • Hardware Requirements: Runs smoothly in any modern web browser with no special hardware needed.

How is it creative?

  • One Connected Mission Loop: Most educational tools teach orbits, rockets, or budgets separately. We link the whole life cycle into one loop (design, Go/No-Go, launch, operate, debrief, redesign), so a weak design choice comes back to hurt the player minutes later in flight.
  • Learning Through Real Stories: Every in-flight anomaly is based on a real event, and Commander Catstronaut turns each answer into a short piece of spaceflight history instead of a simple right or wrong.
  • Cooperative Party-Game Mechanics: Players own roles with competing goals, and timed crises force every role to answer at the same moment, so the crew has to talk to each other, like a real mission control room.
  • Realistic Consequences: Missed launch windows cost more for Mars than for Earth orbit, ion engines can’t make quick burns, and solar panels die in a planet’s shadow. The game rules follow real physics rather than arbitrary penalties.
  • A Real Universe to Fly In: NASA 3D models and imagery of the Earth, Moon, Mars, Vesta, Ceres, Phobos, and Deimos, rendered in real time in the browser.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility: Players have different levels of space knowledge, so we use simple language, guidance that can be switched off, optional hints, and no installation or account.
  • Realism vs. Playability: Missions, rockets, orbits, and events are real, while numbers are simplified so a full mission takes about ten minutes.
  • No Single Right Answer: Each mission was balanced so that several different designs can succeed, while maxing out every option always fails.
  • Meaningful Failure: Players can lose the spacecraft or miss the objective, but the debrief always explains why, turning failure into learning.
  • Team Dynamics on One Screen: Roles, competing goals, and simultaneous crises keep every player involved, even on a shared laptop.
  • Performance and Reach: Everything runs client-side in a single file on ordinary laptops and modern browsers.
